questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the sequence of reform and elections shapes a transition
questions.stem: Explain why the order in which reforms and elections are arranged matters for whether the new order takes root.

answer.exemplar: The two steps answer the same question, who is entitled to govern, in different ways, and the sequence decides which one supplies the pressure for the other. If elections come first, held under the rules that already exist, they may reproduce the previous distribution of power and leave the argument to the winners, who then have no reason to widen the system. If reforms come first, the government that postpones an election has nothing forcing it to concede anything, and a reform passed by the outgoing side is a reform the incoming side may not keep. Sequencing therefore determines whether competition or reform is the pressure that pushes the other, and a transition can be formally complete while the substance of the new order is still contested.

questions.explanation: Reforms and elections settle the same question by different means, so their order decides which supplies the pressure for the other. A wrong sequence can leave the transition formally complete.
questions.hint: Ask what each step does to the pressure for the other.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A constitutional court at a founding moment
questions.learningObjective: Explain the distinctive weight of a founding constitutional court
questions.stem: Explain why a constitutional court established at the moment of founding may matter more than a similar court created later.

answer.exemplar: A court created at the founding moment is given two things that a later court cannot easily obtain. It is asked to interpret a constitutional order that has no settled practice, so its early rulings set the terms on which the new institutions will operate, and every later dispute is argued in the vocabulary the court has established. It is also appointed at the moment when the people who wrote the constitution still hold their authority, which gives its judgments a standing that a later appointment cannot claim. A court created afterwards inherits an existing set of understandings and can only interpret what is already there, however well drafted its statute may be.

questions.explanation: A founding court defines the interpretation of a new order and speaks with the founders' authority; a later court can only work within existing understandings.
questions.hint: Ask what a court sets in place before anyone argues.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how electoral law reform can serve as a tactical instrument
questions.stem: Explain why redesigning the electoral law can be a tactical instrument as well as a technical correction.

answer.exemplar: A new electoral law can be presented as a technical response to malapportionment or a new statistical method, and it may be exactly that. It also redistributes the seats that any given party can expect to win, and the party that stands to gain from the new numbers has a direct interest in producing them. Once the design is written, changing it back requires a further majority and a further justification, so the reform hardens the advantage it created. The telling question is therefore not whether the new rule is defensible, which technical arguments always make it, but whether it was chosen by the party that gained from it and in a way that the losers could not have proposed.

questions.explanation: Redrawing the electoral law alters the seats each party can win, so the design is both a technical matter and an allocation of advantage. Who chose it is the diagnostic question.
questions.hint: Ask who gains seats from the proposed design.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the road to consolidation is uneven
questions.stem: Explain why the road from breakdown to consolidation is often uneven, with periods of apparent normality between the moments of crisis.

answer.exemplar: Between a breakdown and a consolidated order there is usually no continuous sequence of progress, and treating it as one produces wrong expectations about both the risk of reversal and the timing of reform. Consolidation depends on institutions acquiring habits and personnel, and those are built quietly, in stretches when nothing appears to be happening. Reforms are often made in bursts that respond to a crisis and then left alone for years, so the visible record alternates between drama and calm without any change in the underlying direction. A reader who expects steady progress either overestimates the danger in the quiet phases or underestimates the durability of gains that appear minor, and the practical implication is that the quiet years are when the institutions which will decide the outcome are actually being made.

questions.explanation: The record alternates between visible crisis and quiet consolidation because institutions are built in uneventful stretches. The calm periods are when the outcome is decided.
questions.hint: Ask what happens during the periods that look uneventful.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why durability depends on the losing side's position
questions.stem: Explain why the durability of a negotiated settlement usually depends on what happens to the losing side after the agreement.

answer.exemplar: A negotiated settlement is a bargain in which each side gives up something in exchange for something, and the losing side gives up more, namely the chance to govern. What protects the arrangement in the years after the handover is therefore not the defeated party's goodwill but its stake in what has been agreed. If the incoming side keeps offices, budgets, pensions and legal protections for the former rulers, those former rulers have a concrete interest in the settlement continuing, and a change of government would cost them those interests. If the terms are vague, temporary or unenforced, the same stake is absent, and the settlement rests on the calculation that defection would be more costly than compliance, which is a far weaker thing to rely on.

questions.explanation: Durability comes from the losing side retaining a material stake in the arrangement, so that defection would cost it more than compliance. Vague or unenforced terms remove that stake.
questions.hint: Ask what the defeated side gains from continued compliance.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a single index number is a poor summary
questions.stem: Explain why a single index number is a poor summary of how much room an executive has to act.

answer.exemplar: The number hides what the index was built to measure, which is the range of decisions the executive can take without effective challenge. Two countries with the same total may be in very different positions, because one might have an unrestrained judiciary and a fully subordinate military while the other has the reverse, and those combinations respond differently to a crisis. The index also depends on how the components were weighted, and a single total cannot show a movement in one component that is large enough to matter. Reading the index properly therefore means reading the components and asking which of them actually constrains the executive in the situation at hand, not whether the total has risen or fallen.

questions.explanation: A single total conceals which component moved and how components combine, and it embeds a weighting that may not suit the situation. The components and their relevance are what the index cannot show.
questions.hint: Ask what the components tell you that the total cannot.

questions.stem: From the judgment, which inference is best supported?

options.text: The court's first act was to disable a specific instrument of the executive, using the constitution itself
The government accepted the judgment because it had no legal route of appeal
options.misconception: treats a decision not to appeal as proof no appeal existed

options.text: The court's finding shows that it had already established itself as the final arbiter
options.misconception: infers institutional standing from a single judgment

options.text: The reference to a committee shows that the assembly had become the court's superior
options.misconception: reads a referral to the legislature as the court yielding

questions.explanation: The judgment used the constitution to suspend regulations issued without authority, establishing the constitution as binding on the executive. The decision not to appeal shows nothing about appeal.
questions.hint: Ask what the court actually did in its first judgment.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute a proportional seat share under a mixed system
questions.stem: The group's proposal allocates 150 seats proportionally and reserves 15 for a single national constituency, so 135 are allocated by party. A party with 12 per cent of the vote would win how many of the proportional seats under the group's example?
questions.explanation: Twelve per cent of the 135 proportional seats is 16.2, which is the proportional share before the rounding rule is applied. Using all 150 seats would ignore the reserved constituency.
questions.hint: Multiply 135 by the party's share of the vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a two-column diagram of control and constraint
questions.stem: Two columns are placed side by side in the group's diagram. The left column lists signals that the executive is still in control; the right column lists signals that the rules are being applied to the executive. An arrow between the columns points from left to right. What does the diagram ask readers to watch for?

options.text: The moment when the executive loses its formal powers to the courts
options.misconception: assumes a transfer of powers the columns do not describe

options.text: The point at which the opposition has won enough seats to take over the executive
options.misconception: reduces the shift to an electoral arithmetic change

options.text: The year in which the highest number of signals was recorded
options.misconception: reads the arrow as a request to find a maximum

options.text: The gradual shift from signals of executive control to signals of rules applied to the executive

questions.explanation: The arrow links two lists of signals rather than two states of power, so the diagram asks the reader to watch for a change in the pattern of behaviour.
questions.hint: Read the two column headings, not the arrow alone.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a committee report as evidence about untested regions

stimulus.body: The committee visited the four regions in turn and held public hearings in each. It found that regional administrations continued to function, that the electoral commission reported on time, and that in two regions the previous administration had retained its network of local appointments. Its conclusion was that the new order had not been tested in those regions, since no election had been held there.

questions.stem: According to the committee's findings, which conclusion about consolidation is best supported?

options.text: The new order had failed in the four regions, because the previous administration still held appointments
options.misconception: treats continued local appointments as proof of failure

options.text: Consolidation had not been tested in those regions, because no electoral test had taken place
The four regions were politically stable, because the regional administrations continued to function
options.misconception: treats administrative continuity as political stability

options.text: The committee should have recommended new regional elections before the next national election
options.misconception: proposes a recommendation the report does not make

questions.explanation: The report's conclusion is that the regions had not been tested, because no election had been held there, so nothing establishes consolidation or failure in them.
questions.hint: Read the committee's own conclusion.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Group campaigns by the number of demands to find the pattern
questions.stem: The group's table lists six campaigns. Three demanded a single change and obtained it, two demanded several changes and obtained a partial response, and one demanded nothing and ended without any agreement. Which reading is best supported?

options.text: Campaigns with one clear demand were more likely to obtain what they asked for
Campaigns that obtained a partial response were more successful than those that obtained their demand
options.misconception: treats partial success as better than full success

options.text: The number of demands explains the outcome, since every campaign with several demands failed
options.misconception: ignores the partial responses won by multi-demand campaigns

options.text: The table shows that campaigns succeed in proportion to the size of the crowd
options.misconception: invents a crowd size variable the table does not record

questions.explanation: Every campaign with a single demand obtained it and every campaign without any demand obtained nothing, so the pattern supports an association with clarity of aim. The table records no crowd sizes.
questions.hint: Group the campaigns by how many demands they made.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why some settlements are revised and others are not
questions.stem: Why are some negotiated settlements revised within a few years while others are never touched?

options.text: Settlements that are revised were never negotiated in good faith by all the parties
options.misconception: explains revision through the sincerity of the negotiators

options.text: Settlements that are never touched were written into the constitution and are therefore unamendable
options.misconception: assumes a constitutional form makes provisions unamendable

options.text: A settlement is less likely to be revised when each party still benefits from it as it stands
Settlements that are revised were always reached under foreign pressure, which weakens them
options.misconception: invents a cause of weakness that the record does not show

questions.explanation: Settlements that remain in force do so because the parties continue to gain from them; where the balance has changed, revision becomes likely. Legal form is not what explains it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the parties still benefit from the terms.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an early election can leave a transition unfinished
questions.stem: Explain why holding an election before the institutions of the new order exist can leave a transition legally complete and politically unfinished.

answer.exemplar: An election held under the previous institutions produces a legitimate-looking result without establishing the practices that make the new order work. Officials are chosen who have not been selected by its procedures, courts have no experience of the constitutional text, and the electoral commission is the one the outgoing government left in place. The result is a government formally elected under rules that were never tested against the new constitution, so the institutions that should have been built during the transition are built afterwards, under pressure, by the winner of an election that was never designed to produce them. The transition therefore appears complete on paper and remains open in practice, since the untested institutions can be captured or contested before anyone is able to say what the new order requires of them.

questions.explanation: Elections under the old institutions produce a result without testing the new order, so the institutions it depends on are built afterwards and remain contestable.
questions.hint: Ask which institutions the election did not put to the test.
